changes: The italics slant 15°, DIN 16's 75° to the baseline, where they took DINish Italic's 12°. Every italic is drawn again from its upright at the new angle, with the same strokes, corners, dots and bowl balance, and the italic angle and caret slope say 15°. Strokes keep their perpendicular width, so a stroke that already leans gains a little ink: 8.8% at most, against 6.5% at 12°. Italic kerns 'at', Medium and SemiBold Italic 'gj', '[j' and '{j', and Bold Italic 'bx', 'lx', 'ox', 'px' and 'sx'.

Roman numerals, Ⅰ to Ⅿ and ⅰ to ⅿ: 32 new characters in every face, 949 in all. Ⅰ to Ⅻ have feet, as the 1940 DIN 16 and DIN 17 sheets draw I, II, V, X and VIII: DINish's own I stem, V arms and X diagonals, each end crossed by a bar of E's arm weight. Every foot is as long as the stem and Ш's white between two stems, so neighbouring feet run on as one bar, over III and from V into VIII. V and X spread their arms until their feet stand that white apart, so the two are as wide as each other, as on the sheets. Ⅼ Ⅽ Ⅾ Ⅿ are the plain L, C, D and M, and ⅰ to ⅿ are the lowercase letters as DINDOT sets the word.

The specimen's hero sets its claim under DIN and its text under DOT, from the second D's stem to the T's edge, and fits the first screen at 1280 × 720. The Four weights grid ends in DIN 16's angle, as the 1940 sheet ends its slanted alphabet: a line at 15° from the vertical beside the last 6, and an arc marked 75°. The zero panel's knob and lever rims are satin aluminium, so the knob no longer reads as a dark silhouette on the light panel. Every control shows the hand on hover.

The specimen's text now gives facts the page does not show, each once: what DIN 17 and DIN 16 were for, and their stroke, a seventh of the capital height, as in Medium; the zero's dot, the i's, and DIN's plain zero; the languages and their local forms; who drew DIN 1451, D-DIN and DINDOT; and what the download holds. The platform sign and the departure board read Leipzig-Stötteritz.

Two pages join the footer: Credits, with DINDOT's lineage from DIN 16 and DIN 17 and DIN 1451 and the tools that build it, and Font license, a plain summary over the SIL Open Font License 1.1 word for word, the license JetBrains Mono uses too. History runs by date: DIN 16 in 1919, DIN 1451 in 1931 to 1936, DIN 17 in 1938, ISO 3098 in 1976. The character browser fits Ⅷ and the other wide numerals to its preview and lists the numerals under Numbers.

ε is DINish's з turned round, so it has DIN's cut terminals and o's height; it stood half a stroke over the x-height and under the baseline. ς is c's top and bowl, whose stroke runs on at the bottom into its tail, where it was c with a tail laid on and a kinked join. The Four weights section is one grid of the eight faces at one size, DIN 17 upright and DIN 16 italic, after the standards for upright and slanted lettering; each row had turned italic halfway through. A new Zero section turns the dotted zero as a round solid, with levers to show or remove the dot and stop the turn and a knob to step through the weights.

Monotonic Greek, Vietnamese and the Cyrillic of Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Tajik, Tatar and Bashkir are native. 136 new characters in every face: Greek letters with the tonos and dialytika and the Greek punctuation, every precomposed Vietnamese letter with the horn and the hook above, and Ә Ғ Қ Ң Ұ Һ Ҳ Ҷ Ҹ Җ Ҙ Ҫ Ӣ Ӯ Ҡ with their lowercase. Each is drawn from DINish's own stems, bowls, bars and marks in each weight, then rounded, spaced, slanted and hinted like DINish's letters.

Every round dot has the area of DINish's square dot, where it had its width and so 79% of its ink: the i and j dots, the full stop, colon, semicolon, ! and ?, the dieresis and dot accents, the dotted zero and the maths dots. The Regular i dot grows from 74 to 94 units, the full stop from 90 to 104. Dots keep their top or their baseline, so nothing moves.

Bold has DINish Bold's weight again, and grows. The build thinned it by 7 units a side and kept its advances, so it set 5.5% lighter than DINish and the ink it removed became space between letters; it now thins by 3.5. Its letters and proportional figures also widen 2% between their stems, as most families' Bolds widen from their SemiBold: a Bold phrase sets about 1.5% wider than SemiBold, and the counters keep more of their room. Side bearings and tabular figures keep their width. Bold Italic follows.

σ is o's bowl with its top run on as the bar. It was o with a bar laid over it, so o's overshoot met the bar in a notch and the bar ran a quarter of the x-height past the bowl. Now one flat line runs from the bowl to the bar's end, 8% of the x-height past the bowl, and σ is about as wide as o. τ and π end in t's own stem and foot instead of a drawn hook, and the Greek lowercase stands at each weight's own x-height.

Greek kerns like the Latin letters of the same shape (Το, ΑΤ), DINish's own Vietnamese letters and È É Ê take their base letter's kerning, Т and Г are kerned apart from Ъ and Ҡ, and η's descender continues n's stem. usWinAscent and usWinDescent rise to 1.1 and 0.3 em, so hinted Vietnamese capitals do not clip in Windows GDI; browsers and macOS keep their line spacing.
The character browser shows Vietnamese, Greek and Cyrillic groups.

Figures, punctuation and signs follow their weight, as letters have since 0.20.0: each takes its own weight's DINish advance, where 0.20.1 gave them the widest weight's. In Regular the figures had set up to 9% wider than DINish's, the comma and full stop 11 to 12% and the quotes 20%. “Revenue rose 6.1% in September, to €208,008.” now sets 2.0% wider than DINish in every weight, against 3.8% in Regular before.

Tabular figures and the data forms keep one advance in every weight, so a table value keeps its width when it turns bold or italic. A value in default figures now grows when it turns bold, as in DINish: €208,008.50 by 3.1 px at 16px (DINish 3.0).
Outlines, kerning, the 576-unit tabular figures and every OpenType feature are unchanged. Each italic takes its upright's advances, as before.
The specimen page can be read in German, with German samples, and the character browser shows ẞ beside ß.

C and c end in DINish's own terminals again, rounded like every other corner. From 0.16 to 0.20.0 the build cut both back with a vertical line, which left a flat on the outside of each terminal, so the letters looked sliced off. Their accented forms, Cyrillic С and с, and the italics follow.

Tighter spacing. Each letter now takes its own weight's DINish spacing, where 0.19 gave every weight the advance of its widest DINish weight, and the word space is DINish's again (0.16 to 0.19 made it 28 units wider). “Dot, your AI Data Analyst” sets 1.5% (Bold) to 1.7% (Regular) wider than DINish, against 3.0% to 5.3% in 0.19.1.
Letter shapes other than C and c, kerning, the 576-unit tabular figures and every OpenType feature are unchanged. Each italic takes its upright's advances, as before.
